titre: The Benin Bronzes: One Museum Returns Them, One Cannot
accroche: In 1897, the British army looted the Benin Bronzes. In 2022, an American museum returned twenty-nine of them; the British Museum cannot.
contenu_vulgarise:
In February 1897, a British army column, about one thousand two hundred men under the command of Rear Admiral Harry Rawson, attacks Benin City, capital of the Kingdom of Benin, in present-day Nigeria. The expedition, mounted in retaliation after the deaths of several members of a British mission a month earlier, destroys the royal palace and forces the Oba, Ovonramwen, into exile. Amid the ruins, soldiers find thousands of brass and ivory plaques and figures, accumulated over centuries by the royal court's craftsmen. Between three thousand and five thousand pieces, by various estimates, leave the country in the following weeks; the British Foreign Office resells a large share of them to cover the expedition's costs.

## Two museums, two laws

More than a century later, these objects are scattered across dozens of Western museums. The British Museum alone holds about nine hundred of them, the largest single collection in the world, but its trustees cannot return them, even if they wanted to: the British Museum Act of 1963, a law passed by the British Parliament, bars its trustees from permanently disposing of any object in the collection, except in a small number of narrow cases. A 2005 ruling by London's High Court confirmed how strictly this principle applies, in a different case: heirs of a Jewish family dispossessed by the Gestapo in 1939 sought the return of four old master drawings, and the court held that the museum had no legal power to give them back, however strong their moral claim.

The Smithsonian, in the United States, does not face the same problem. Its museums are overseen by a Board of Regents, which can change its own rules without an act of Congress. In April 2022, the institution adopted an ethical-returns policy, and on October 11 of that year, the National Museum of African Art returned twenty-nine bronzes to Nigeria's National Commission for Museums and Monuments. The Smithsonian's secretary, Lonnie Bunch, put it this way: "Our possession of these collections carries with it certain ethical obligations."

## One question hiding another

The difference between the two museums is therefore not primarily a difference of will. The British Museum may want to return its Benin Bronzes without having the right to, until Parliament changes the 1963 law; the Smithsonian was able to act on its own because its own structure allowed it to. The question "should this museum return the object it holds?" often conceals, without saying so, a narrower and less visible one: does it, strictly speaking, under the law that governs it, have the power to? Two museums can answer the first question differently without ever having disagreed on the substance.

quiz.question: Why can't the British Museum return its Benin Bronzes, when the Smithsonian did so with its own in 2022?
choix: Because the British Museum believes the bronzes rightfully belong to it
Because the Nigerian government has never officially requested their return
Because a 1963 law bars its trustees from permanently disposing of an object, except in narrow exceptions
Because the British Museum's bronzes do not have the same origin as the Smithsonian's
quiz.explication: The British Museum Act of 1963 bars trustees from disposing of objects in the collection, except in very specific cases; a 2005 court ruling confirmed how strict this is, even for works stolen by the Nazis. The Smithsonian, by contrast, simply changed its own internal policy in 2022, without needing an act of Congress.
